utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Blaskic, can you hear me? The Prosecutor's Office? My dear colleagues? Fine. You can all hear me. The public can hear me as well. So we can start. Let us identify, first of all, the various parties. The Office of the Prosecutor, please, to start with.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. My name is Mark Harmon and I am assisted today by my colleague, Mr. Andrew Caley.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. The Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. Russell Hayman and my colleague, Anto Nobilo, appearing for General Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You are the new counsel for the Defence for General Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Do my colleagues have any questions? No. Fine. This hearing is dealing with several items. The first item relates to the application for amendment of the indictment following the order by Judge McDonald on 22nd November 1996, order by which the indictment was reviewed and amended. Therefore, to be in compliance with our Rule 50(B) of our Rules, we should ask the accused whether he pleads guilty or not guilty for the various counts of the indictment, following which the Chamber is seized with various applications. Some of them are underway. The first one relates to the question of protecting witnesses, the full disclosure of which has been requested by the Prosecution. We are talking about Witness (C), and we need to settle this matter, following recommendations made to the Witness Unit which was to send an investigator on the field. There is a new litigation revolving around the date to be set for the trial; following this time an application for an adjournment coming from the Prosecutor's Office and the Defence reacted to this motion. The Chamber was seized with very recent written briefs. We received the translation thereof only last night regarding the motion to compel the production of various discovery materials. This is a request by the Defence and there is still no answer regarding this motion coming from the Prosecutor's Office. In order to respect the logical and chronological order of the proceedings, let us first deal with the indictment. First of all, I wish to turn and address the Prosecutor's Office. We examined the indictment and we examined every count. I noted various differences. There were some specifications as to the location, long indictment periods, more precise counts. But, first of all, I would like to ask the Prosecutor whether the indictment that gave rise to the amendment ordered by Judge McDonald, whether that is a new indictment or does it replace or modify the former indictment. Before I turn to General Blaskic, I wish to see some precision, some specifications from you. Are we dealing with a completely modified indictment on the basis of which the Prosecution and the Defence will organise their proceedings? How can you explain this to us?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, the original indictment which was filed in November of last year contained 13 counts. The amended version which you now have in front of you contains 19 counts. Count 10 in the original indictment has been dropped from the charge sheet, so that is no longer in the indictment. We have added, the Prosecutor has added, seven new counts. I can, if you wish, go through and identify with you each and every change, but if you want a simple answer to your question, the changes that have been made are substantial amendments, although some of the original charges, many of the original charges, that were contained in the original indictment remain extant within this new indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DESCHENES
utterances.text: So what happens? Do we have to work with two indictments, the original and the amended one, or does the amended one completely replace the original one? What is the position?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, the order that was made by Judge McDonald was that the original indictment remains extant in respect of the other accused, except for General Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DESCHENES
utterances.text: We are only concerned today at the moment of speaking with one accused, General Blaskic. In that connection, what is the position now?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: This is the new indictment, your Honour, in respect of General Blaskic. This is the indictment which replaces the old indictment filed in November of last year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DESCHENES
utterances.text: I see. So now we forget the old indictment, call it that way, and we have as a working document the new or amended indictment?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: That is right, your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DESCHENES
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, dear colleague. Everything is clear now. Before I turn to General Blaskic, is everything clear for the Defence? Are the explanations set forth by the Prosecutor clear? I am not asking for arguments but just for a piece of information. Are you clear on everything?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Their position is clear, your Honour, but I question whether technically the original indictment has been dismissed as to General Blaskic, because unless it has been dismissed there are still two indictments before the Court, so I would think simply as a technical matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DESCHENES
utterances.text: Do you not think that is really highly technical? As I was saying, that appears to be highly technical. Really, we are not here to discuss a procedure but the substance of the charges that have been laid against your client. You as well as we know what the indictment contains in its new form. So we are told that the new replaces the one. That is the position taken by the Prosecutor. If that be so, for one ‑‑ I am just giving you my personal opinion ‑‑ I would be prepared to take the old indictment and tuck it in the back of the file and forget about it. We have this new indictment which does contain, indeed, all the substance of the former one, but for one count, count 10, which has been dropped from the amended indictment. So that being so, I think that you and us, we all know what the position is, and whether or not you have a technical dismissal matters little, it seems to me, with respect to the substance.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I do not mean to be hypertechnical, your Honour, but there are a number of factual allegations in the original indictment that have been dropped. With respect ‑‑‑‑

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DESCHENES
utterances.text: If that be so, the Prosecutor will have to be held with his statement that the new indictment contains everything that the Prosecutor wants to bring as a charge against your client. I would suppose that if the Prosecutor now would want to bring evidence that would be wandering outside the terms of the amended indictment, you would object and there would be a high possibility of that objection being maintained.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: We would and I wanted to note that on the record for all to comment and, if the Prosecution does not agree, I would invite or ask through the Court them to say so so we could further resolve that issue.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, dear colleagues. We all agree. The indictment filed today by the Prosecutor (as confirmed by Judge McDonald) is replacing count 10. 17 new counts have been added to the new indictment. Counsel and the Prosecution will base their litigation before the Court on this new indictment. In keeping with the joint Rules, Rules 50 and 52, I am now turning to General Blaskic, as was done at the initial appearance. However, we have to proceed in the same fashion again. Can you confirm, General Blaskic, that you were able to take note of the indictment in your own language as well as the official languages of the Tribunal? Another mandatory mention has to be the mention of whether you plead guilty or not guilty on the basis of this new indictment, or are there any counts where you plead guilty and other counts where you plead not guilty? General Blaskic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Your Honour, I received the new indictment in the language that I understand. I have read it and I understood it completely. I plead not guilty and this is all I have to say in this moment.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You are, therefore, pleading not guilty. The Trial Chamber takes cognisance of this and this will be taken note of in the proceedings. You can sit down. Let us now move to another item on the agenda; the date to be set for the trial. I wish to remind you of the calendar of proceedings we had previously established. On the basis of our previous decision of 2nd October 1996, we had ordered that within 15 days of the decision, i.e. 17th October, disclosure would be made to counsel and their client of the decision 17.17 that had been transmitted to the Defence in its redacted form by 1st December. Another 10 statements had to be made known to the counsel. This is part of a major litigation that has been exposed in front of the Court on various occasions. Regarding the date for the trial, in the decision of 12th October, we had set a time limit of 60 days for preliminary motions possibly presented by the Defence and this is expiring on 16th December. Lastly, the Trial Chamber set the date for the beginning of the trial on 8th January 1997, Wednesday. Regarding the date to be fixed, to be set, for the trial, we have to deal with this again, not that the Trial Chamber wants to change its decision, but the Trial Chamber noted that there is a request for adjournment for the date beginning the trial. In other words, the trial would start, according to the motion, on 21st April 1997. This is being challenged by the Defence. We are going to hear both the Prosecution and the Defence on this point. On the other hand, the Defence has to express its views and considerations for time limit for preliminary motions, provided they want to file preliminary motions. The Trial Chamber regarding the first point is going to give the floor to the Prosecution for them to present their application for adjournment of the beginning of the trial. Thereafter, the Defence will indicate whether they plan to file preliminary motions within the time limit up to 16th December. Thereafter, the Trial Chamber will be in a position to determine the date for the beginning of the trial, should we decide not to stick to 16th December. Prosecutor, you have the floor regarding the date that you wish to apply for the beginning of the trial, i.e. 21st April. You have the floor, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, your Honour. We have filed with this Court an application for an adjournment in this case. In our request, we have asked that the trial date be adjourned until 21st April 1997. The reasons that we have set forth for this application are clearly spelt out in our application itself. Going to the background, first of all, of the indictment itself: When the indictment was filed, this indictment was filed under Rule 47, and the standard set forth under Rule 47 is that there must be reasonable grounds for the Prosecutor to believe that the accused has committed a crime within the jurisdiction of this Tribunal. That standard, the standard enunciated in Rule 47(A) as well as the standard set forth in 18(4), is a standard that is not equivalent and does not mean conclusive evidence or evidence beyond a reasonable doubt. I would refer the Chamber to a decision that was rendered by Judge Sidhwa in the case of Rajic, that is case No. IT‑95‑12‑1. Specifically, your Honours, I would refer the Court to pages 7 and 8 of that opinion in which Judge Sidhwa discussed the meaning of a prima facie case. Counsel for the accused in his motion has indicated that the investigation of a case ends when the matter is submitted to the Judge for confirmation. That is incorrect. The Rule, Rule 47(A), your Honour, envisions both a lower standard, that is the standard I have just said, sufficient evidence to provide reasonable grounds for believing that a suspect has committed a crime within the jurisdiction of the Tribunal, and it also envisions that additional investigation post indictment will continue. I said ‑‑‑‑

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DESCHENES
utterances.text: May I intervene here? Assuming that you are right, let us assume you are right in your legal proposition, that there is a difference in the level and the nature of the evidence that has to be brought in support of the original indictment and then the level of the evidence that would be necessary in order to bring a conclusion of guilt. Let us assume that for the purpose of discussion. What strikes me is that the indictment was actually confirmed roughly a year ago or thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That is correct, approximately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DESCHENES
utterances.text: But the fact is that now you say that a year afterwards you are still not in a position to go on at the date fixed already some time ago on 8th January. I am rather surprised by that, however be the merit of your contention as to the difference in the level of evidence that is necessary. Do you not think that a year afterwards it is high time that the Prosecution be in a position to proceed, and it is high time that the accused knows exactly where he stands?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, my answer to that would be, clearly, if this was a very small and narrow case, one year, under the facts and circumstances of this case and the investigative needs of this case, would be more than sufficient to prepare this case for trial. That is not the case with this indictment. This case, your Honour, involves a series of crimes committed in a land that is far away, that has been investigated vigorously by this Prosecution Office within the limits of its resources. The crimes are extremely complex and spread over a wide geographic area. I would point to number of decisions of other courts, your Honour, that indicate in terms of the length of time necessary to investigate a case. Clearly, it is a function of the complexity of the case. If it is a simple case, it should not take and will not take very long to investigate. If it is complex, however (as is this case), then the investigative needs and requirements to make a case trial ready are considerably different. That is what we assert with our motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DESCHENES
utterances.text: Could I be a little more ‑‑‑‑

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Excuse me, I think we need to have a full explanation by the Prosecutor on his motion or application. Thereafter there will be a reaction from the Defence, thereafter the Tribunal, the Judges, will raise all relevant questions. Please go on with your legal argument and your factual argument on the various points, including your response to the observations made by Judge Deschenes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is, I think, the statutory and regulatory background and that is found in Rule 47(A) and Article 18 of the Statute. At the time this indictment was presented for confirmation, the Prosecutor filed a Prosecutor's certificate which is part of the record in this case. That Prosecutor's certificate was filed on 2nd November 1995. In that, Richard Goldstone, who was the Prosecutor of the International Criminal Tribunal, indicated that he was filing his certificate and he says as follows: "I, Richard Goldstone, Prosecutor of the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia, pursuant to my authority under Rule 47 of the Tribunal Rules of Procedure and Evidence, in the course of an investigation am satisfied that there is sufficient evidence to provide reasonable grounds for believing that the suspects listed above have committed a crime within the jurisdiction of the Tribunal. Notwithstanding that the investigation is continuing, I hereby transmit the above indictment with the attached supporting material to a Judge of the Trial Chamber of the Tribunal for confirmation in accordance with Article 19 of the Tribunal's Statute". That investigation, as I have indicated in this motion, is continuing with all due speed and deliberation and in good faith. I have set forth in the course of this motion, and I will not reiterate what is set forth in this motion, factors that compel us to make this request for an adjournment. In respect, your Honours, of the motion in opposition filed by the defendant, the defendant has asserted that (and I am referring to page 1) once the indictment is confirmed the investigatory phase of the case is concluded. That is simply not correct. The Rules, as I have said, indicate that the investigation, the low standard enunciated in Rule 47 and Article 18.4 envision that the investigation will, in fact, continue. Again, the defendant asserts on page 2 of his motion, lines 18 and 19, that the formal investigation process concludes upon confirmation of the indictment. His premise, as I have said, is not correct. The Prosecutor, contrary to what is asserted in the Defence motion, your Honour, is not saying it does not have a prima facie case. If that were the case, we would withdraw this indictment. So, I want to make that perfectly clear. In respect, your Honour, of the defendant's motion requesting that there is no basis for the Court to permit an adjournment, I would refer to the Court's inherent powers in controlling proceedings, and inherent in their powers is the right to set trial dates and reset trial dates. Lastly, your Honour, I would like to comment, if I can be permitted to do so, on the defendant's application to be released. If this is the appropriate time I am prepared to do so; then I will do so, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes, Prosecutor, can I summarise your presentation? You acknowledge ‑‑ we need to agree on your concluding remarks ‑‑ you are not ready. You are not currently in a position to undertake the beginning of the trial on 8th January 1997. That is the main point, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The Court will decide on the basis of the legal standards but, factually speaking, you are not in a position to uphold your indictment against General Blaskic by 8th January? This has to be clear for my colleagues and for myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That is correct, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Fine. The legal question arising, which may be subordinate to another factor, is that there was confirmation of the indictment in November 1995, and you add to your application a challenge on the legal standards, the Court will decide, but beyond the question of knowing whether on the day of the initial appearance the Prosecutor must be ready to start the trial, the day after, beyond the sort of semantical litigation, there is a very sound legal argument based on the standards we use in this Court. The Court knows that there was confirmation of the indictment a year ago. I am turning to the Defence for their response to the Prosecutor's application. The Judges will then raise any relevant questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. As far as we have been able to understand, the Prosecution has said it is not ready and that it does not have enough evidence and they request further investigation. If the Prosecutor says that, we agree, it means that the case should go back to the stage of investigation. If the case is to be brought back to the stage of investigation, our defendant is to be set free. I could not agree that the level of quality of evidence should be beyond any reasonable doubt for the indictment to be issued and to start the trial. The grounds for suspicion is all that is required, and the evidence should have the quality, should be beyond reasonable doubt at the stage when the Trial Chamber renders a judgment. According to the Statute of this Tribunal and the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, as far as I know of almost every country in Europe, there are stages in the proceedings: there is an investigation, the preindictment proceedings, the confirmation of the indictment and the trial, the main hearing. According to the motion of the Prosecution, the stages are being mixed here and the Defence deems that it is not possible. One of the basic rights of the defendant before this Tribunal is the right for a fair and expeditious trial. Our defendant, having heard that an indictment had been issued against him a year ago, about eight months ago or maybe even more, had voluntarily (as the only defendant to do so) appeared before this Tribunal, because he believed that he would be given the right to a fair and expeditious trial and that he would be able to clear his name. However, after one year the Prosecution claims it is not ready, and they connect their possible readiness for trial to some future events. So now we have to ask ourselves the question: How the Prosecution is able to know whether they would be ready in three months, in 10 months or a year? The investigation did not start a year ago. The investigation started before that. The investigation ended a year ago, and this period from the first confirmation on the indictment, it was some extra time that was given to the Prosecution to enable them to prepare their case. The Defence believes firmly that the Prosecution is not ready, and we believe that they will not be ready for the simple reason because we believe that our client is innocent. So, we move that the motion of the Prosecution not be granted, and that we start with the trial, as this Trial Chamber envisioned, on 8th January 1997. If the Trial Chamber decides that the case should be taken back to the stage of investigation, we agree that it be done but then, according to the Statute of this Tribunal, there is the option that the Prosecution withdraws its indictment and in that case we move that our client be set free. He appeared voluntarily before this Tribunal and he is ready at any time when the Prosecution is ready, in six months, in a year, in two years, three years, to appear voluntarily before this Tribunal again. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Let me now turn to my colleagues and see if they have questions. Let me remind you that there are two points, turning to the Defence, on which I think we ought to make a decision: first of all, the deadline to file the preliminary motions. For the time being you have not said that you would want to reject any preliminary motion. You know that there was date of 60 days starting from 16th December. So I do not know what you intend to do about it. The other part is that there are seven new counts on the indictment. So it maybe a while, yes, you could challenge the issue that, well, whether the trial should start the day after that date, but I think that there was at least a deadline of 60 days that should run for the case when further preliminary motions may be filed. But let me turn to my colleagues and see if they have questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DESCHENES
utterances.text: I have a question to Mr. Nobilo and subsequently a question to the Prosecutor. Mr. Nobilo, do I understand you correctly that your main point today is that you say that you are ready to start the trial on the assigned date, that is to say, 8th January?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Of course, we are ready.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DESCHENES
utterances.text: Right. You do not foresee any obstacles, for instance, the emergence of new procedures on your part that may prevent the Tribunal from starting its proceedings on 8th January?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: No, we see no obstacles for the beginning of the trial and, of course, we cannot foresee how the trial is going to progress.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DESCHENES
utterances.text: Right. Thank you very much. I would have just a complementary question to the Prosecutor: I have not seen in your application for a postponement the reason why you suggest April 21st. Could you tell us why that date rather than any other one?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I suggested that date for a number of reasons. The first reason was because there is another case that will be starting, that is the case of Delalic et al. for trial, that it is envisioned that the Blaskic case and the Delalic case would be tried simultaneously. That means that there would be abbreviated weeks in respect of each of those trials. I checked with my colleagues who are responsible for Delalic case to find out their best estimate of when that case would conclude. That was one reason but not the first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DESCHENES
utterances.text: That is a matter of logistics. It is a matter for this Tribunal to make the necessary arrangements.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I understand, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DESCHENES
utterances.text: I am afraid to say so, you cannot foresee now that because of another case this one might find some troubled waters to navigate in. I suggest that that does not appear to me to be a very strong reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am responding to your question as to my reasons. I am trying to give them all to you. That was one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DESCHENES
utterances.text: Let me say that the first reason does not appear to me to be very strong.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. I am not giving you the reasons necessarily in order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DESCHENES
utterances.text: I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The other reason was I considered certainly the disruption of the holiday season. Clearly, December is a month where availability of witnesses, frankly, is extremely difficult. I projected in discussions with my investigative staff how long they thought it would take to conclude the investigation, that is, attempting to locate other witnesses that we have identified. It included translation of documents that we have received, how long that would take. Ultimately, I selected the date of April 121st based on those considerations, based on the needs of the investigation. That is my best estimate, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DESCHENES
utterances.text: Do you have any other strong reasons?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Obviously, the strongest reason, your Honour, is the need to complete this investigation and the assessment that we have made is that it will take until that date, or shortly before that date, to complete the investigation. That is the strongest reason I have to offer this Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DESCHENES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You are welcome.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Turning to Judge Riad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, if I remember rightly, you had suggested to start in February last time and we decided to have it in on 8th January. I suppose that you are were ready to start in February, as far as the first indictment was concerned. Now you made it clear that in the new indictment that the new indictment, in fact, has absolved the first indictment, but you have seven new counts. Did I understand rightly?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That is correct, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: This new period, is it related to these seven new counts?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Certainly in part, but not totally, your Honour. Since the trial date was selected or it was proposed by the Prosecutor's Office, that is February, there have been some events that have impacted on our ability to present the case by January 8th. As I mentioned in my motion, as a result of a decision taken by this Chamber in relation to protective measures, approximately 19 witnesses of ours are no longer willing to participate in the trial. So we have had a major disruption in that respect. Subsequently, we have also received documents, voluminous documents, that need to be translated, that need to be analysed, and that has also been significant in terms of our assessments of this case. So at the time the Prosecutor who was responsible for this case suggested a February 1st date. He did not have before him the new factors I have outlined in our application for an adjournment. I have set forth reasons that are post that September discussion between the Prosecutor's Office and this Trial Chamber as to the selection of a proper trial date. I have tried to articulate those in this application that we have filed with the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So you claim that there is a substantial change of circumstances?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That is correct, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: That is the real reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That is the reason, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You mentioned in your motion that you have problems in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, in September, because of security reasons, we were unable to send investigators into the field. I have mentioned that in my motion as well. Those security reasons are reasons that clearly are disruptive and should, and I think must, be taken into consideration in considering the amount of time it has taken to investigate this case and get it in a trial ready state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You are welcome, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Before I give the floor to the Defence on preliminary motions, I would like to put things in context. We talked about potential provisional release. We are not there yet. I do not think that it is for the Tribunal to do that today. I do not think there is a formal request on this. The Tribunal should have to set the date of the commencement of trial first. Mr. Prosecutor, of course, I do not want to take a stance because it will be for the Tribunal to do that, I think that the arguments about the potential availability of a courtroom or the facts that may affect the proceedings in the world, I do not think that should affect the running of the trial. Let me turn to the Defence and see if you have observations on what the Prosecutor said. Then I would like to answer you the question that was asked by Judge Deschenes. I feel that you have not fully answered the question because when Mr. Nobilo says that he does not see any obstacles that may prevent the trial from commencing on 8th January, I think he has failed to answer the issue on preliminary motions. Let me remind you that the deadline is on 16th December for that. Of course, if you say that you do not have any preliminary motions, it is different from saying that you have preliminary motions, and see whether you have many or not many, whether you want to bring an answer to the seven new counts. All of this is required for the Tribunal to see whether we maintain the date of 8th January for trial commencement or see whether a new date is applicable. The floor is yours, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. I will address the issue of preliminary motions. If I may first briefly address the most recent comments by the Prosecutor? He has stated that the holiday season requires a delay in the commencement of trial because of the inconvenience to witnesses and perhaps others. Our client will be in custody during the holiday season, your Honours, and it is incumbent on everyone, including witnesses, to make themselves available a week before a holiday or the week after, whatever. I submit that is absolutely no reason to delay the trial so that others can have an uninterrupted period of four or six weeks or perhaps three months to enjoy one or more holidays. Also the Prosecutor argued that he spoke to his staff who said they needed this period of time to 21st April in order to translate documents and locate witnesses. I submit that is a black box answer. That answer comes out of a black box. There are no objective facts provided to this Tribunal from which the Tribunal can evaluate whether there is a reasonable basis for that position. It is simply a bit of information coming out of a black box and it cannot be given weight by this Tribunal. I submit that the Prosecutor has told us he has a prima facie case. What is a prima facie case? A prima facie case is a case which at the close of the Prosecutor's evidence if the Defence brought a motion for what we call, at least in the United States, a directed verdict of not guilty, the Court drawing all inferences from the evidence in favour of the Prosecutor would deny that motion and go forward. That is, at least in our system, what prima facie case means. I can refer the Court to the American Law Institute and other sources and case law for that. That means there is a basis for the Prosecutor to go forward. So when he says he is not ready, it is not that he does not have sufficient evidence to take the trial forward and potentially, in his view, to prevail. It means he wants more evidence. He seeks for strategic and tactical reasons to improve his chances of winning. Of course, we all do. We would all like to have more time and more opportunities to enhance our ability to win for our client, but that is not grounds to delay the case. He also suggested that the seven new counts in the indictment are a reason for delay. If one compares the two indictments, one will see that the subject matter, with the exception of the extended time period and one new geographic area, is the same. So they have broken it down into new numbers, but it is the same material, the same subject matter, persecution of civilians, etc. etc. So seven new counts is a red herring. There are no new substantive charges that are factually new before this Tribunal. In any event, Rule 50 provides that after an amended indictment there can be a delay so that the accused can have adequate time to prepare. They are supposed to know what the new charges are. They are supposed to have investigated them. Delay in the case of an amended indictment is for the accused's benefit because it is news to us. That is why we, if we ask for it, need time to prepare. We are not asking for time because the charges are not new. Next he states that there are 19 witnesses who do not want to testify and that is a reason for a delay. I can understand a request for a delay of a day or two if a witness is having difficulty travelling or some other personal accommodation needs to be made, but the fact is there are witnesses who are not going to be willing to testify in this case. We submit it is because they know that General Blaskic was committed to a joint defence against the Serbs of Croats and Muslims together, and they are not willing to come and testify against him for that and similar reasons. We also have been told by the Prosecutor that there are voluminous documents and that requires a delay. Where did these documents come from? When did they ask for these documents? Did they delay in asking for them? Did they ask for them in November 1995? How do we know they are not going to ask some other group or organisation or nation state for more documents in March and come in here and in April, on 20th, and say, "We have just got five new boxes of documents"? There are no objective facts before this Tribunal that would permit a delay on any of the grounds proffered. With respect to the subject of preliminary motions, we filed last week a motion to compel the production of discovery materials and we are hoping to have that addressed on an accelerated basis. We filed two preliminary motions this morning. They have not made it to your Honours, of course. I hand carried them with me from my office. One of them is a motion to strike portions of the indictment pertaining to failure to punish liability, that is, liability for failure to punish individuals under the accused's command, who are alleged to have committed war crimes. The other motion is a motion in limine to determine the mens rea or intent requirement for command responsibility. These motions were filed this morning. They are in English.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you, could you please just specify the points of law for Rule 73 which you are referring to? Obviously, members of the Tribunal have not had a look at them because you filed them this morning. Could you please be specific? Rule 73 provides for very specific cases of preliminary motions. I am sure that you can moderate them. Can you please help us out with them, specifying them?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The first motion regarding failure to punish liability is a motion that the Tribunal lacks jurisdiction over any asserted offence constituting liability for failure to punish subordinates, because any such purported offence is not a crime at customary international law. The jurisdiction of this Tribunal is limited to crimes under customary international law. So the first motion I referenced is a motion on jurisdiction. The second motion is a motion in limine litis for a decision, requesting a decision, by the Tribunal of what the mental standard is, the mens rea or intent requirement is, for command responsibility, because why is it important that that be determined before trial? The accused has a right to know what is the legal standard being applied to him at his trial. He cannot be told that at the end of the trial. He must be told that at the beginning or, at least, before the trial begins, so that he knows what the standard is and what the test is and he can intelligently, with the assistance of his counsel, defend himself against the charges. The indictment does not specify what the mens rea or intent requirement is, not with sufficient specificity. So with respect to what extent the schedule for preliminary motions is implicated here in this question, the question of a delay in the trial date, I would submit that since certainly my first appearance in the case in September before the Tribunal, the Defence has bent over backwards to move the case along. We agreed, offered to waive our 60 day period starting from the date at which all documents would have been translated. We have now filed three preliminary motions weeks before the deadline ‑‑ weeks before the deadline. They are all in English. One of them has been in a week. The Prosecution can start working to respond immediately. We will have some number of additional preliminary motions, whether there is one or two or three, I cannot tell the Court yet. There certainly will be one, a motion challenging the indictment based on vagueness, which is a universal concept the defendant is entitled to fair notice of the charges and where that notice is not provided the indictment should be stricken. One of the grounds ‑‑ I can go ahead, it is no secret, and preview it to provide some flavour ‑‑ is the amended indictment extends the time period of the alleged offences by an entire year, from May '93 to May or so of '94. That is a time period that was not included in the prior indictment. There are no specific acts alleged by anyone during that time period in the amended indictment. So there is a year of potential liability. We do not know what act anyone committed, much less committed by our client, that we are going to have defend against in the trial. Certainly we are going to bring a motion that the indictment, as at least to that time period, should be stricken to vagueness. We are still looking at other areas for potential motions. I can say there is one other motion we certainly are working on that has come into my mind now, and that is a motion challenging the jurisdiction of the Tribunal over grave breaches provisions due to the lack of an international armed conflict in the theatre in question, between the parties in question. The motions that we have filed to date, the three we have filed, are by far the lengthiest motions that we will file. The remaining motions will be shorter, quite frankly, simpler and more straightforward, I think. So, in terms of the date for trial, I would urge the Tribunal to consider the extent to which the Defence has gone the extra mile, if you will, to get our lengthier motions in early so that we can stick to the date of January 8th. Can I say that there is no potential reason out there that may arise for some delay. Is it possible I could come in in two days and say we have another motion that has just come up? All I can say with respect to that issue ‑‑ I think that was your Honour's question, perhaps ‑‑ is we have not yet received the supporting material filed with the amended indictment. So we do not know what is in there. Of course, it is possible there is some in there that we would need to address in a preliminary motion, but I can tell this Tribunal we will endeavour very vigorously to meet the December 16th deadline. As of right now, we certainly intend to meet it. As to the other motions I mentioned regarding international armed conflict and vagueness, those motions will be in by December 16th. We are going to make that deadline and I submit that it is reasonable to expect the Prosecution to take a month ‑‑ a month is a fairly long time ‑‑ to reply to each of these motions as they come in, and for us to have a few days to respond in a written opposition. That should put us around January 8th when the papers are all in. Of course, the Court should have some time to consider them all, although the papers will have been coming in ‑‑‑‑

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Hayman, for interrupting again. I feel that my colleagues are as surprised as I am. I do not think you can state publicly everything in the opposite, on the contrary. You cannot say both that you are ready for 8th January and make the statement that you made, while at the same time claiming that what you have filed on the motion, you know, compelling the production of evidence which you have filed just a few days ago, I received it on my desk ‑‑ it was not completely translated, by the way ‑‑ just last night; you have filed two preliminary motions, one on jurisdiction and you have announced two more, I understand in total there would be four preliminary motions, then you say that it would take about a month to respond, to take due note of this. I mean, this is December. The deadline is 8th January. You cannot say both that there is nothing new in the indictment ‑‑ I mean that is what you said earlier ‑‑ there is nothing new, there are new elements, while claiming that you need a preliminary motion to respond on the time frame, you know, the additional time frame on one that is a reproach to your client. I think that we are all in good faith. I think that this is the reason why I wanted to raise the issue of preliminary motions. If there are four preliminary motions, which are fairly important, they are not just formal, I mean, one is on mens rea, the other one in limine litis, one on jurisdiction, and you also recognise that it will take about a month for the Prosecutor to respond, so I do not think that it is realistic to say that you are ready to start on 8th January. I think that my colleagues feel the same way, but Judge Deschenes wanted to add something, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DESCHENES
utterances.text: I just wanted to say on this question of deadline, I not only share the views of the President and the surprise that you have just expressed, and the hesitation on the fact that the trial may commence on 8th January. It is one thing for the Defence, I mean, the Defence is entitled to file preliminary motions, that is one thing, but it is another thing for the Prosecutor to ask for sufficient time to respond. It is the Prosecutor's right, and it is also another thing for the Tribunal to hear the various parties and a fourth thing for the Tribunal to ask to have some time to think the matter over. This, unfortunately, will certainly delay the start of the trial much later than 8th January.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I just would like to ask, Mr. Hayman, also about his demand for discovery. Do you not think that will also require some time?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. It is lengthy but I think it will take less time to resolve in the sense that the Prosecutor's response is likely to be either, "We do not have any evidence in this category", or "We have it and we will produce it voluntarily" or "We have it but we do not, for example, think it is exculpatory", in which case there may be review by the Court or something like that required. It is less legal than just a factual issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Which requires time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: It certainly will require some time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Heaps of paper and perhaps translation too?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Translation of what, your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Of some of the documents, perhaps, to English?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: They may be true but, as I stated earlier, it has been asserted there are voluminous new documents, but we have been told nothing about whether they were diligently pursued and gathered or only recently requested and obtained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: They are voluminous, as you have said, or as you have been told?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: We have been told. I do not know what that means in the Prosecutor's mind, but that is the word he has used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Are you more or less aware of the time you need for all these preliminary, the four or five, the one on the intent requirement, in limine litis, or you aware how long it would take from you and from us and from the Prosecutor to answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Of the five I have identified, we have already filed three. We have two more to file. We will certainly get those in before 16th December. Then, quite frankly, it is for the Tribunal, of course, to set a schedule so that those motions can be heard and resolved in an orderly fashion. I do not presume to usurp that function of the Tribunal, but I can say that the Defence has done everything it can to move the process forward quickly. We will continue to do so. I would urge that we not delay the trial date on the grounds that it may require a lengthy period of time to resolve motions. If that is the Tribunal's conclusion, seeing the motions and hearing from the Prosecution, that there has to be some delay, that is the Tribunal's prerogative and we certainly will abide by any direction from the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, I would like to remind you of the fact that there is at least one statutory time limit, that is the 60 days, and from this day there is a new time limit. Today is 4th December, so this brings us to 4th February. I know you are going to state that you are not intending to use that time limit, but you reminded us of the contradictions of the Prosecutor's Office, but you yourself or your predecessor said that you were not going to use the 60 day limit or that would be used moderately. The Court notes (and it is your right) that you are bringing motions until the time limit of 16th December. So we have to show realism, be realistic, and we all, all parties, wish to move the process forward as fast as possible to come to a ruling on General Blaskic. This being said, as was reminded by Judge Deschenes, the Trial Chamber needs to have time for response. So think of the new time limits. There is 4th February to be observed as of today. This being said, unless you have some supplementary objections, I think just about everything has been said as to scheduling dates, but you wanted to intervene again, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The date of February 4th, if I may, your Honour? Your Honour, the Defence waives any 60 day period from today. We are not seeking it; we do not want it. We will have all preliminary motions in by 16th December.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The Registrar will have to see to including this in the minutes. I mention the Registrar ‑‑ how far have we got, Registrar, with translation? It is all fine and well to set schedules from the bench, but there are other types of logistics. There is the availability of courtrooms, but there is also the question raised by the very basic demand made by General Blaskic to have all the documents translated in his language. Could you give some indications or ask questions so that everything be clear as to the date for trial?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARRO
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Some very brief observations since, needless to say, the Registry is at the disposal, at the service, of the whole Tribunal. I would like to bring before the Court the fact that we received three files yesterday. Here they are. They are documents handed in by the Prosecutor's Office. The Defence has received that in English, I suppose, but this has to be translated into the defendant's language. I am sorry to say that these documents are coming in late. We will have to do everything that is possible, but we need at least three weeks to a month. Given this time of year, it is more difficult to have translations being done, but we will act diligently. The second remark, regarding supporting material to the new indictment, I do not know whether the supporting materials are the same or whether we are going to receive new supporting materials. This is beyond our control so far. For the proceedings to be clear and for communication to take place properly, I would like to state that we say, whatever the ruling of the Trial Chamber be, the two trials, the Delalic and the Blaskic case can run concurrently, simultaneously. The layout suggested so far is that we could have two‑and‑a‑half days of hearing for each case. As to the appearance of possible witnesses, it is true to say that 8th January is a problematic date. Over a month ago, I filed a written brief with the Prosecutor to call his attention to this. We have problems booking flights for the beginning of the year.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Registrar. In spite of the goodwill displayed by everybody and, regardless of the substantial matters raised by the Prosecutor's motions for adjournment until 21st April, there are other considerations to be looked into, including those related to the Defence, your possible preliminary motions, that is. We are going to suspend hearing for half an hour. We will resume in closed session as to the protection of Witness C. To the extent of which ‑‑ I mean, is this still a topical question, protection for Witness C? Are you still upholding your application regarding protective measures for Witness C? If you so desire, we will have a hearing in closed session on the measures to be applied to Witness C. As is suggested by my colleague, we will resume in public session in order to communicate the decision, but there is still outstanding the question of the protective measures. As to the other matter, the production of material, this a preliminary motion and it will be connected to the other preliminary motions. There is still the question of the Witness C. What is your view on this, Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I respond to you after the brief recess in regard to Witness C and the protective measures sought?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: If I understand properly, this recess is something that is wished by all parties, including the Judges. There is a recess. We will resume again in 30 minutes time.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We resume our work. Please let the defendant come in. Mr. Harmon, a preliminary question: I thought it was implicit in the discussions, but you do not have any preliminary motion you want to file with the Court, do you?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No, your Honour, we do not.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Fine. Therefore, it is going to be stated that there are no preliminary motions coming from the Prosecutor's Office. The time limit for the Defence preliminary motion will be set at a time limit for 16th December. This being so, the Judges have looked again at the schedule or the calendar for the proceedings, organising only the calendar for preliminary motions, since it is impossible to foresee anything beyond the calendar for preliminary motions. This is our decision. The four or five preliminary motions, major on the merits, will be ready for translation for all parties on 10th January 1997. We will ask the view of the Registrar on this date. In order to gain time, the Prosecutor will have one month starting, not from 10th January 1997, but from the time when the Prosecutor has knowledge of the preliminary motion in one of the languages of the Tribunal, i.e. English. So the time limit will start on 20th January. This means that the Prosecutors will have up to 20th January to respond to the five substantial preliminary motions that will be filed with the Court by the Defence. The Defence will have up to 3rd February 1997 to respond to the Prosecutor's arguments as a sort of rebuttal, as is currently done now in our Court. Translation shall be made available to all parties and to the Trial Chamber. The Registry will need two weeks, 14 days, that is, up to 17th February 1997. Due to constraints connected to the fact that we are in plenary sessions in March, the hearing on preliminary motions will take place on 12th March at 2.30 in the afternoon and will, if necessary, last until 13th and 14th March. It did not seem necessary or useful to the Trial Chamber to provide for an even provisional calendar for the trial, but I believe that both the Prosecutor and the Defence can envision the date for the beginning of the trial. This is subject to any litigation related to the Trial Chamber's decision. We will need a few weeks to make a ruling. So you can imagine when, approximately, we could start the trial for General Blaskic. To date, we are not setting any date for the beginning of the trial. There will be a hearing on preliminary motion on 12th, 13th and 14th March. Another trial will have started by then, and we will use the courtroom the previous days. I am now turning again to Mr. Harmon. There is one item left on the agenda, that is, the explanations or submissions on the protection of Witness C, following the latest development relating to the protective measures. The Registry has sent a notice. I would like to raise this question. Do you plan to present a position to the notion of protection of the witness? If you so desire, it will be in closed session. Do you plan to present deliberations or submissions?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, thank you very much. No, your Honour, we have reviewed the recommendation of the Victims and Witness Unit in relation to Witness C. We are now withdrawing our application for protective measures in relation to Witness C. Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Fine. We take due note of the withdrawal of your application for protective measures for Witness C. This being so, we will adjourn the meeting, unless you have final remarks? The Prosecution? The Defence? Mr. Hayman.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Just two things, your Honour, and I will ask Mr. Nobilo to address some issues concerning conditions of confinement. Let me also just raise, the Tribunal may have ruled, but we were seeking some earlier schedule on the discovery motion because it is possible that our motion for discovery could result in the production of new material to us which we would rather not receive on the eve of trial. I just wanted to make sure. I know the translated motion was only just received by the Tribunal last night, but that would be our request, that if possible we somehow accelerate that motion, so that if there is new material we will get it sooner rather than later. That is the only issue I had and then Mr. Nobilo had one other item, your Honours. (The learned Judges conferred).

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Prosecution, are you ready to present your submission to this motion by the Defence? In which case we could set a hearing for this afternoon to make it possible for the Defence that comes from far abroad to be able to present its submission. Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, regrettably, I am not prepared at this point to respond. I am in the process of preparing a response. I received this motion on Friday afternoon. I have obviously started my response and will be prepared to file that response next week. At the earliest possible time, your Honour, I could file response with this Chamber by Friday but, realistically, given the breadth of that motion I could file it probably early next week.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hayman, is it necessary to have a hearing, you seem to be in a hurry, or when could you be back? Is it necessary to have full deliberations before the Court? You filed a motion. We are waiting for a response by the Prosecution. If you so wish, the Trial Chamber could try and hasten the development of the process. We could provide you with a written response, a ruling, by way of an order to be given early January in order to speed it up. But if you insist on presenting your submission, needless to say you will be heard, but what do you feel about this?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: May I suggest this. Depending on what the response of the Prosecution is, we do not know and it is difficult to anticipate whether a hearing will be necessary. My experience in these kinds of motions in the past is frequently a hearing is helpful because the question is, how is a certain piece of evidence potentially exculpatory or helpful to the Defence? The Prosecution may likely say in their reply that this evidence is not helpful, and it is incumbent on us, the Defence, to articulate why we believe a particular piece or type of evidence is helpful. I plan to be back in The Hague the week of January 6th. Perhaps, if I may suggest, if a hearing is not necessary then the Court can and should rule whenever convenient for the Court, but if a hearing is necessary and if we persist in our request for a hearing having seen the Prosecution's opposition, any time that week would be convenient. Quite frankly, I will be here and I will make myself available when it is convenient for the Court. We feel this is important and we would like to press ahead with it.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. I simply point out that it is difficult to establish the schedule. It is important to be clear on the development of the process. Of course, we are at your disposal, at the disposal of the parties, for the trial to be conducted impartially, this is our job, our mission, but also at the earliest convenience. Prosecution, you will file your briefs this very week or next week? Next week is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The next week, your Honour. (The learned Judges conferred).

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We take due note of the observations made by Mr. Hayman. We note that you will be present on 6th January. Possibly could we have a hearing by the end of December or the week before Christmas? I do not know at all, but I am raising the question. Of course, the Prosecution is available, but it may be more difficult for the Defence. You may wish to have a fresh look at the arguments put forward by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: May I, your Honour?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If the Prosecution's brief is filed, say, by the middle of next week, maybe 11th, I would think a hearing on 16th or 17th, if necessary. That is certainly doable and it would give everyone time if it could be translated. I guess that is the question, and not knowing the length of their filing, then there is the question of translation.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I suggest we do not make a decision right now. Maybe the Registrar wants to add something.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARRO
utterances.text: Even if you file the motion on 11th it all depends on the breadth of the motion. We will do our utmost, of course, but I do not wish to provide you only with draft documents. It all depends on the date at which we receive the brief and the number of pages covered.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So we decide not to make any decision. We took note of everybody's dates. We know that Mr. Hayman will be present on 6th January. We know that all parties, including the Court, wish to have a hearing before the end of this year, but there are other contingencies, including contingencies on the part of the Registry that have to be taken into account. We do not make any decision on the date of hearing. We do not know whether it is going to be necessary to have a hearing. It may be sufficient to have an exchange of written views. If the parties wish to have a hearing, obviously enough there will be a hearing. Mr. Nobilo, you wished to take the floor to make a few observations?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I have a proposal. It is obvious that there will be several weeks, maybe even months, until the beginning of the trial, and I would like you to consider the possibility of modifying the conditions of detention of General Blaskic in his current place of detention. At this time he is not allowed to go out in the fresh air, but only he is allowed to do some sports activity for one hour a day. Our proposal, in order to keep him in shape before the trial, is to allow him two hours a day of sports activities and two hours a day access to the open air, to the garden in the place where he is detained. We would also like, if possible, for his wife and his children to be allowed to stay here for a longer period of time, at least two weeks every months, until the beginning of the trial. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo, let me recall what you already know. It is for the President of the Tribunal to decide upon the conditions of detention of the defendant. General Blaskic is detained under conditions which were laid out in an order which is not under the jurisdiction of the present Chamber. I therefore invite you to turn to the President of the International Tribunal and to make this request. It will be for him to make a final decision on that. Unless there are further observations ‑‑ let me turn to my colleagues to check ‑‑ then the meeting is adjourned. 12.10 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: (The hearing adjourned for a short time)
